# James 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## vv. 1–6: Denunciation of the Wicked Rich

### v. 1 — “Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you.”

James opens with a prophetic denunciation, not an invitation to repentance. Commentators widely agree these are **unbelieving rich**, not Christian brethren. Unlike earlier sections addressed to “brothers,” these are not called to repent — only to “weep and howl” at coming judgment.

- **Ellicott** notes the phrase “Go to now” (Ἄγε νῦν) is the same as in James 4:13 and sees this as concluding the section begun there. “Wailing” (ὀλολύζοντες) is a picture-word imitating the cry of anguish, unique in the NT but used in the LXX for prophetic doom (e.g., Isaiah 13:6; 14:31). He sees the primary reference as the impending destruction of Jerusalem, but with similar judgments included. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Precept Austin**, citing Hiebert and others, observes these rich are “apparently not believers.” James does not condemn riches themselves (cf. Prov 10:22) but the wickedness that so often accompanies wealth. The “miseries” (plural) refer to final judgment, not temporal troubles. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-5-commentary

- **Guzik (Enduring Word)**, citing Poole, says: “He speaks to them not simply as rich (for riches and grace sometimes may go together) but as wicked, not only wallowing in wealth, but abusing it to pride, luxury, oppression, and cruelty.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Gill** introduces the chapter saying James “reproves the vices of rich men, and denounces the judgments of God upon them.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

---

### v. 2 — “Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes.”

James describes three kinds of wealth perishing: stored food (rotted), garments (moth-eaten), and precious metals (corroded, v.3). Each perishes in its own way.

- **Guzik**: “Stores of food are corrupted (rotted), garments are moth-eaten, and gold and silver are corroded. Each one of them comes to nothing in their own way.” The point is that hoarded, unused wealth decays. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Ellicott**, quoting Bishop Wordsworth: “Your wealth is mouldering in corruption, and your garments, stored up in vain superfluity, are become moth-eaten: although they may still glitter brightly in your eyes… they are loathsome in God’s sight; the Divine anger has breathed upon them and blighted them.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Precept Austin**: The imagery underscores the transitoriness of wealth. Quoting Spurgeon: “That only is worth my having which I can have for ever. That only is worth my grasping which death cannot tear out of my hand.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-5-commentary

---

### v. 3 — “Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days.”

Gold in pure form does not corrode, so this is figurative — their wealth is as worthless as if it were rusted. The “rust” becomes both witness and executioner.

- **Ellicott**: The precious metals themselves do not corrode, “but the base alloy does, which has been mixed with them for worldly use and device. The rust of them shall be a witness to you: not merely against, but convincing yourselves in the day of judgment; and, moreover, a sign of the fire which shall consume you.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**, quoting Moffatt: “With a Dantesque touch of horror, the rust will devour (or corrode) your flesh like fire, you are so bound up with your greedy gains; your wealth perishes and you perish with it and by it, eaten away in burning pain.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Precept Austin** explains “in the last days” refers to the days of grace given for repentance, which the rich used instead for hoarding. Citing Eccl 5:15: “As he had come naked from his mother’s womb, so will he return.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-5-commentary

- **Ellicott** defends the apostles from the charge of delusion about Christ’s imminent return: “The simple explanation is an old one — the potential nearness of Christ… His actual return was probably nearer in the first ages of faith than in the brutality of the tenth century.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

---

### v. 4 — “Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.”

The specific sin: defrauding day-labourers by withholding wages. OT law required prompt payment (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14–15). James uses the Hebrew title “Lord of Sabaoth” (Hosts/Armies) — the warrior God who defends the oppressed.

- **Ellicott**: “Not merely the wrong of the poor, but the wages kept back from him by the niggardly master, contrary to the merciful Jewish law (Leviticus 19:13), which permitted no delay in payment whatever.” The title “Lord of Sabaoth” is “a sublime and awful picture” — God seated as judge to hear the charge. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**: “The title Lord of Sabaoth… means ‘the Lord of armies,’ especially in the sense of heavenly and angelic armies. It describes God as the warrior, the commander-in-chief of all heavenly armies.” The use of this title gives the unjust rich “a sober warning.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Precept Austin**: The rich “got rich by defrauding their laborers (who had no legally binding contracts with their rich employers), as many men have done throughout history. But God will not be mocked.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-5-commentary

- **Gill** lists this as the third sin of the rich: “their injustice in detaining the hire of labourers from them.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

---

### v. 5 — “You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter.”

The rich lived for pleasure while ignorant of impending doom, like cattle fattening themselves on the very day they will be slaughtered.

- **Ellicott**: “The pleasure and wantonness wherein the rich had lived, the selfishness with which they had cared for their own hearts, in a time of death for others — nay, preparation of like for themselves: this is the aggravated wrong.” The Passover that drew rich Jews to Jerusalem became their own slaughter under Titus. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**: They “lived indulgently without regard for others (as the man in Jesus’ story about the rich man and Lazarus, Luke 16:19–31).” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Precept Austin**: The imagery of “fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter” is that of cattle being fattened for the butcher, unaware of their fate. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-5-commentary

---

### v. 6 — “You have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you.”

The climax of their sin: the rich used their power to condemn and kill the righteous (τὸν δίκαιον). The righteous person did not resist — a mark of Christlike meekness.

- **Ellicott** notes the striking parallel to Christ: Peter called Jesus “the Holy One and the Just” (Acts 3:14), Stephen spoke of “the coming of the Just One” (Acts 7:52). James himself was called “the Just” and was martyred — “James the Just prophetically described his own murderers.” The final words “he doth not resist” describe “the behaviour of himself, as of every real witness for Christ.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** asks: does this refer to Christ? At first it seems so, but the language also draws from Isaiah 3:10 (LXX) and Wisdom 2, making it “a prevalent practice of the wicked rich in every age.” It applies to Jesus, Stephen, James son of Zebedee, and soon James the author himself. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**: “Often those who are poor and without power in this world have little satisfaction from justice. Yet God hears their cries, and He is the one who guarantees to ultimately right every wrong.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

---

## vv. 7–12: Patient Endurance Until the Lord’s Coming

### v. 7 — “Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil — how patient he is for the fall and spring rains.”

James pivots from denouncing the oppressors to comforting the oppressed believers. “Therefore” (οὖν) ties the patience exhorted to the certain judgment just declared. The farmer waits for both early rains (Oct–Nov, softening ground for ploughing) and latter rains (Apr–May, maturing the crop).

- **Guzik** lists ten ways the farmer’s waiting parallels Christian endurance: he waits with reasonable hope, a long time, working all the while, depending on things beyond his control, with his eye on the heavens, despite uncertainties, encouraged by the harvest’s value, because he has no other option, because giving up does no good, and aware of how seasons work. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Ellicott**: “Be sure God’s help is nigh… ‘The darkest hour is on the verge of day.’” The early and latter rain were “only two seasons of rainfall in the Holy Land, and, if long delayed, famine was a certain result.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik explicitly rejects** an allegorical reading of “early and latter rain” as outpourings of the Holy Spirit: “There is no allegorical picture here of an early and a latter outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the church.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Gill**: The exhortation is to patience “from the instance of the husbandman waiting patiently for the fruit of the earth, and the rain to produce it; and from the consideration of the coming of Christ, the Judge, being near at hand.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

---

### v. 8 — “You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near.”

Repeats the call to patience, adding “strengthen (establish) your hearts.” The nearness of the Lord’s coming (παρουσία) is the ground.

- **Ellicott**: “The presence of the Lord is nigh. For the ancient belief in the nearness of Christ’s second advent, see Note above on James 5:3. The word used by the Apostle to describe its closeness is the same as that used in Matthew 3:2, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**: “There is a real sense in which the coming of the Lord was at hand in the days of James as well as in our own day today. One might say that since the Ascension of Jesus, history has been brought to the brink of consummation and now runs parallel alongside the edge of the brink.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Pulpit Commentary**: “Stablish your hearts (comp. 1 Thessalonians 3:13).” The coming of the Lord draws near — “So Isaiah had announced (Isaiah 13:6), ‘The day of the Lord is near (ἐγγὺς ἡμέρα Κυρίου).’” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/5.htm

---

### v. 9 — “Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door!”

Under hardship, believers are tempted to grumble against each other (κατ’ ἀλλήλων — “against one another”). James warns that the Judge (Christ) is already at the door.

- **Ellicott** corrects the KJV “grudge”: “Say in preference, *Murmur not*. ‘Grudge’ has curiously changed its meaning from an outward murmur to an inward feeling.” He contrasts Revelation 3:20, where Christ lingers mercifully at the door, with this verse where He comes as Judge. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**: “Jesus comes as a Judge, not only to judge the world, but also to assess the faithfulness of Christians (2 Corinthians 5:10). In light of this, we cannot allow hardship to make us unloving towards each other.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Ellicott** adds the haunting historical note: one of the mocking questions put to James by his enemies before his martyrdom was, “Which is the door of Jesus?” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

---

### v. 10 — “Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.”

The OT prophets endured mistreatment yet persevered. Jeremiah especially is noted: put in stocks (Jer 20:2), imprisoned (Jer 32:2), lowered into a miry dungeon (Jer 38:6).

- **Ellicott**: “These are the bright ones in the cloud of witnesses, of whom the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebrews 12:1) speaks” — Daniel, Jeremiah, Elijah, Zechariah, Isaiah, Urijah, John. “Thus the saints of the Old Covenant are held up for honour and imitation to those of the New.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**, citing Poole: “As much as God honoured and loved them, yet they were not exempted from afflictions, but were maligned, traduced, and persecuted by men… and therefore when they suffered such hard things, it is no shame for you to suffer the like.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

---

### v. 11 — “See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.”

Job is the supreme example of perseverance (ὑπομονή). The “outcome from the Lord” (τέλος κυρίου) shows God’s purpose was compassionate, not cruel.

- **Ellicott** provides a lengthy reflection on the book of Job: “Job’s friends were so certain of his misdeeds, that they would not hear his self-defence… We know Job was innocent; God Himself bears witness to it (Job 1:8).” Job attained to the faith that “to serve him and love Him is higher and better than any mundane welfare, though it be with wounded feet and bleeding forehead, or an ash-heap and filthy sores.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik** notes three things about Job: (1) his perseverance (Job 1:20–22); (2) the “end intended by the Lord” — God had a good purpose, as a surgeon’s knife differs from an attacker’s knife; (3) the Lord is “very compassionate” — the Greek (πολύσπλαγχνος) literally means “many-bowelled” or “great-hearted,” indicating deep tenderness. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Guzik**, quoting Spurgeon: “He who tested with one hand supported with the other. Whatever Satan’s end might be in tempting the patriarch, God had an end which covered and compassed that of the destroyer.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

---

### v. 12 — “Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath. Simply let your ‘Yes’ be yes, and your ‘No,’ no, so that you will not fall under judgment.”

James echoes Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:34–37. The issue is not all oath-taking (God Himself swears oaths; oaths appear in both Testaments) but deceptive, frivolous, or evasive oaths used to avoid truth-telling.

- **Gill**: “Of such sort of swearing, and of such oaths, is the apostle to be understood; otherwise an oath is very lawful, when taken in the fear and name of God… James manifestly refers to Matthew 5:34.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

- **Ellicott**: Jewish practice had “many subtle distinctions” between binding and non-binding oaths. “All such subterfuges are utterly condemned; and further, every word which breaks the letter or spirit of God’s Third Commandment.” He defends judicial oaths by noting Christ Himself answered an oath before Caiaphas (Matt 26:63–64) and cites Article 39 of the Church of England: “a man may swear, when the magistrate requireth, in a cause of faith and charity.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/5.htm

- **Guzik**: “The need to swear or make oaths, beyond a simple and clear yes or no betrays the weakness of one’s word. It demonstrates that there is not enough weight in one’s own character to confirm their words.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Guzik** also notes Moffatt’s suggestion that this verse may seem out of context: “Probably James jotted it down as an after-thought, to emphasize the warning of James 5:9; in excitement or irritation there was a temptation to curse and swear violently and profanely.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

---

## vv. 13–18: Prayer, Healing, and Confession

### v. 13 — “Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises.”

In every circumstance — suffering or cheerfulness — the response is to turn to God. The suffering pray; the cheerful sing psalms (ψαλλέτω).

- **Gill**: “The afflicted he advises to prayer; and those in comfortable circumstances of body and mind to singing of psalms.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

- **Guzik**: “James has the same advice for both the suffering one and the cheerful one: take it all to the Lord. In fact, the two commands could be reversed: sufferers should sing also, and the cheerful should also pray.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Pulpit Commentary**: “Prayer in the narrower sense of petition is rather for sufferers, who need to have their wants supplied and their sorrows removed. Praise, the highest form of prayer, is to spring up from the grateful heart of the cheerful.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/5.htm

---

### v. 14 — “Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.”

**This is one of the most debated verses in James, with significant differences across traditions.**

The sick person (κάμνοντα, implying serious illness — the person is bedridden and must “call for” the elders) takes the initiative. The elders (πρεσβυτέρους τῆς ἐκκλησίας) pray and anoint with oil “in the name of the Lord.”

**On the meaning of “anointing with oil”:**

- **Medicinal view**: Oil (specifically olive oil) was widely used as a medical remedy in the ancient world (cf. Luke 10:34; Isaiah 1:6). The Greek word here for “anoint” (ἀλείφω) is distinct from the ceremonial/religious word (χρίω). Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) strongly advocates this: “Oil was and is frequently used in the east as a means of cure in very dangerous diseases… St. James desires them to use natural means while looking to God for an especial blessing. And no wise man would direct otherwise.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Symbolic/consecration view (Reformed/Evangelical)**: The Gospel Coalition’s Samuel Emadi argues the oil is neither medicinal nor sacramental but “simply symbolizes consecration to God, as it often does elsewhere in Scripture (cf. Num. 3:3; 1 Sam. 10:1; Ps. 89:20). Anointing with oil is a physical act expressing a spiritual truth: we belong to God and have committed ourselves wholly into his care.” He rejects the medicinal view because in Mark 6:13 the healings are supernatural, not medical. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/anoint-sick-with-oil-james-5/

- **Sacramental view (Roman Catholic)**: The Catholic Encyclopedia states this verse provides the biblical foundation for the Sacrament of Extreme Unction (Anointing of the Sick). They argue: “The expression *tous presbyterous*, even if used alone, would naturally admit no other meaning” than the hierarchical clergy. “The words ‘in the name of the Lord’ here mean ‘by the power and authority of Christ’, which is the same as to say that St. James clearly implies the Divine institution of the rite he enjoins.” The anointing is a true sacrament: oil as remote matter, anointing as proximate matter, prayer as form, conferring grace. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05716a.htm

- **Dummelow’s Commentary** (Anglican): “It was, and is, a Jewish custom for a sick man to make his confession to some rabbi or rabbis… St. James is telling his readers that this custom was to be continued by Christian Jews, and that the confession of the sick man was to be made to the clergy (‘presbyters’) of the Church. They would then (1) pray over him for the pardon of his sins, and (2) anoint him with oil (the recognised remedy, Isaiah 1:6; Mark 6:13; Luke 10:34).” He adds: “It is scarcely necessary to point out that the Roman Catholic doctrine of Extreme Unction receives no justification from this passage. In the Prayer-Book (‘Office for the Visitation of the Sick’) the lines laid down by St. James are closely followed.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/james-5.html

**Contrast between traditions on the elders/priests:**
- **Catholic**: “Let him bring in the priests of the church” — ordained clergy administering a sacrament.
- **Protestant**: The elders are the spiritual leaders of the local congregation, not a separate sacerdotal class. Guzik says the Roman Catholic Church “mutated this command to anoint the sick into the ‘sacrament’ of Extreme Unction, administered to someone to prepare that one for death. Something James intended to heal was made into a preparation for death!” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

---

### v. 15 — “And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.”

The “prayer of faith” (ἡ εὐχὴ τῆς πίστεως) saves (σώσει) the sick, the Lord raises him up (ἐγερεῖ), and sins are forgiven. The interpretive question is whether this guarantees physical healing.

- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic)**: “The context of the statement demands that James does not exclude physical healing as an answer to prayer, though he does seem to mean something broader than only a physical healing. We should pray for others in faith, expecting that God will heal them, then leave the matter in God’s hands.” He adds: “many are not healed simply because there is no prayer of faith offered.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Reformed (TGC/Emadi)**: “The beginning of verse 15 seems to suggest that ‘prayers of faith’ inevitably result in physical healing. Certainly, such an interpretation doesn’t accord with reality. Godliness is no guarantee of physical health, nor can it perpetually deter death (Heb. 9:27). Furthermore, Paul himself, perhaps the most faith-filled Christian ever, had to leave Trophimus sick in Miletus (2 Tim. 4:20).” The “saving” and “raising up” point toward the ultimate resurrection. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/anoint-sick-with-oil-james-5/

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist)**: “The prayer of the elders, being put up in faith by them, and in which the sick person joins by faith; such a prayer is a means of bringing down from God a blessing on the sick man, and of restoring him to his former health.” He notes that forgiveness “he shall have a discovery, and an application of pardoning grace to him: and indeed the removing the sickness or disease may be called the forgiveness of his sins, which is sometimes the sense of this phrase in Scripture, as in 1 Kings 8:34.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

- **Catholic**: The effects are both bodily and spiritual. The Catholic Encyclopedia argues that the words “save” and “raise up” carry “this twofold meaning,” and “it is much more natural in the present context to suppose that they do convey it.” Bodily healing is “a conditional and subordinate end.” — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05716a.htm

---

### v. 16 — “Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.”

Confession here is mutual (ἀλλήλοις — “to one another”), not auricular confession to a priest. The healing (ἰαθῆτε) may encompass both physical and spiritual dimensions.

- **Guzik**: “Mutual confession and prayer brings healing, both physically and spiritually. Confession can free us from the heavy burdens (physically and spiritually) of unresolved sin, and removes hindrances to the work of the Holy Spirit.” He specifies this confession is “not to a priest, but among believers” and “should be specific, discrete, and made to those sinned against.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Pulpit Commentary (textual note)**: The reading “οὖν” (therefore) has overwhelming manuscript support (א, A, B, K, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic) over the Received Text’s omission, confirming the logical link: because sins may be involved in the sickness, mutual confession is needed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/james/5-16.htm

- **Gill**: “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

- On “the prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail” (ἐνεργουμένη — “energized, at work”), the phrase underscores that it is not mere words but the active, working prayer of a godly person that accomplishes much.

---

### vv. 17–18 — “Elijah was a man just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.”

Elijah illustrates that extraordinary answers to prayer come through ordinary people. “A man just like us” (ὁμοιοπαθὴς ἡμῖν — “of like passions/nature with us”) emphasizes his shared humanity.

- **Guzik**: “Elijah was an ordinary man with a nature like ours, yet his earnest prayers moved heaven itself — showing that we too can be powerful in prayer when our hearts align with God’s.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- **Gill**: “Elias, whose prayer, though a man subject to like passions as other men, against, and for rain, was very successful.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

- The reference to “three years and six months” (also in Luke 4:25) matches the 3½-year drought in 1 Kings 17–18, though the OT account does not specify the exact duration; Jewish tradition supplied this figure.

---

## vv. 19–20: Restoring the Wanderer

### v. 19 — “My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back…”

James returns to the “brothers” address. “Wander from the truth” (πλανηθῇ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας) does not necessarily mean losing salvation, but straying into doctrinal or moral error.

- **Gill**: “Christians should not only be concerned for the health of each other’s bodies, but also for the good of their souls; wherefore, whenever it is observed that any are straying from the path of truth, methods should be taken to restore them.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

- **Guzik**: “We should confront those who have wandered from the truth and seek to turn them back.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

---

### v. 20 — “consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins.”

The one who restores a wanderer “saves a soul from death” and “covers a multitude of sins.” This is a powerful motivation for the ministry of restoration.

- **Gill**: “Whoever is the happy instrument of such a restoration is the means of saving a soul from death, and hiding a multitude of sins.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/james-5.html

- **Guzik**: “We should confront those who have wandered from the truth and seek to turn them back, knowing that in doing so we save a soul from death and cover a multitude of sins, restoring what was lost.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-5/

- The phrase “cover over a multitude of sins” echoes Proverbs 10:12 and 1 Peter 4:8. Interpreters differ on whose sins are covered: the restorer’s (as an act of love covering his own sins), the wanderer’s (sins forgiven through repentance), or both. The traditional reading generally sees the wanderer’s sins as covered through forgiveness upon repentance.

---

## Summary of Key Tradition-Specific Differences

**James 5:14–15 — Anointing with Oil and Healing**

| Tradition | Understanding |
|---|---|
| **Roman Catholic** | Sacrament of Anointing of the Sick (Extreme Unction). The “elders” (presbyters) are ordained priests; the anointing confers grace, forgives sins, and may restore bodily health conditionally. |
| **Reformed/Evangelical (TGC)** | Oil is symbolic of consecration to God. Healing is not guaranteed; the passage points toward ultimate resurrection. |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik)** | Physical healing is expected through the prayer of faith. Many are not healed because no prayer of faith is offered. Oil may be medicinal or symbolic; elders represent church leadership. |
| **Anglican (Dummelow/Ellicott)** | Oil is a recognised remedy combined with prayer. The Prayer Book follows this pattern in the Visitation of the Sick. Not a sacrament; not Extreme Unction. |
| **Reformed Baptist (Gill)** | Prayer of faith is the means; healing and forgiveness are both in view. Oil seen as part of the practice but secondary to prayer. |

**James 5:19–20 — Saving a Soul from Death**

The question here is whether the “death” in view is physical death (as a consequence of sin), spiritual death (eternal judgment), or both. The traditional Protestant reading generally sees it as deliverance from both temporal judgment and eternal death through genuine repentance, while maintaining that true believers cannot finally apostatize (perseverance of the saints). The Catholic reading sees this as consistent with the possibility of mortal sin and restoration through the sacrament of penance. Arminian/Wesleyan traditions see it as evidence that believers can fall away and be restored.
